country.comment: Primary empirical/regulatory case study is in Alabama, United States (four Black Belt counties—Hale, Lowndes, Perry, and Wilcox—with an in-depth institutional trace of Uniontown in Perry County, alongside broader US discussion of Appalachia, Texas, California, and North Carolina). Sections 1-5 also provide comparative philosophical, constitutional, and secondary policy background on Western Europe and North America (including France, Italy, Spain, Canada, Mexico, and England/Wales).
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 9-20, Sections 5-6

effect_estimate.comment: No inferential regression or causal effect estimate is computed; findings consist of descriptive administrative enforcement counts, self-reported overflow volumes, E. coli sample concentrations, and secondary county sanitation prevalence statistics (e.g., 65% and 93% unpermitted household sewer systems in Hale and Wilcox counties cited from Elliott et al., 2017).
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Constitutional review finds no Western European or English-speaking North American constitution explicitly protects a human right to water or sanitation (only Mexico in North America does). In the Alabama Black Belt case study, chronic municipal mismanagement and regulatory enforcement collapse by ADEM persisted despite a 2002 violation notice, a 2005 civil complaint, a 2008 consent decree requiring remediation within 3 years, and 76 non-compliance citations (2005-2018): ADEM reissued NPDES discharge permits in 2008 and 2012 and approved an unsuitable second clay-soil spray field (halted by a 2014 Stop Work order after $4.4 million in USDA grants), resulting in ongoing sewage overflows exceeding 1.25 million gallons from the Uniontown lagoon (Dec 2017-Jan 2019) and >1 million gallons from the spray field in 2018 (7,300-11,000 cfu/100 ml E. coli vs. the 4,000 cfu/100 ml NPDES daily maximum).
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 3, Section 1; PDF p. 6, Section 3; PDF pp. 14-18, Section 6; Figure 1, PDF p. 16

mechanism_certainty.comment: Capped at 2 by non-experimental/non-quasi-experimental design ceiling. Assigned 2 because Section 6 directly documents the administrative and regulatory enforcement mechanism in Uniontown through primary agency records (2005 civil action, 2008 three-year consent decree, 76 non-compliance citations, 2008 and 2012 NPDES permit reissuances despite violations, permitting on unsuitable clay soils, 2014 Stop Work order, and unpoliced industrial dumping) operating on ongoing municipal wastewater treatment failure and sewage discharges.

mechanism_flags.comment: Central mechanism is regulatory ENFORCEMENT failure in Uniontown: non-compliance citations, violation notices, NPDES/SID permit non-enforcement, and administrative Stop Work order (sanction), plus the 2005 civil lawsuit and 2008 binding consent decree (judicial_review). Also examines poor regional/engineering planning and unpermitted household systems (planning), municipal water plan boundary exclusion in Tooleville/NC (ELIGIBILITY, service_area), and fragmented governance structures across municipal, state, and federal entities (institutional_fragmentation).
mechanism_flags.value: ENFORCEMENT, ELIGIBILITY, sanction, judicial_review, planning, service_area, institutional_fragmentation
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 10-11, Section 5; PDF pp. 12-20, Section 6

outcome_flags.comment: Examines sanitation_access and water_access throughout; service_quality (fecal/E. coli and BOD contamination from sewage overflows, raw sewage in homes, drinking water standard violations); formal_connection (unconnected households using straight pipes or unpermitted/unlicensed septic systems in Appalachia and Hale/Wilcox counties); and service_coverage (exclusion of minority/low-income communities from municipal water service plans and boundaries).

publication_year.comment: Published in Azafea. Revista de Filosofía 21, 2019, pp. 129-157 (received March 29, 2019; accepted June 28, 2019).
publication_year.where_found: PDF p. 1, journal header and reception/acceptance dates

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Study combines constitutional/international-law analysis with an empirical institutional-regulatory case study grounded in administrative dockets (ADEM notices of violation, civil action complaint, 2008 consent decree, NPDES permits, 2014 Stop Work order, 76 non-compliance citations, SSO filings, and USEPA diagnostic audit), fitting none of the six conventional epidemiological or qualitative interview designs.
risk_of_bias_tool.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 2-3, Section 1; PDF pp. 14-19, Section 6

sample_size.comment: No formal participant or survey sample size is reported because the article is a philosophical essay paired with a documentary regulatory case study rather than a sampled empirical survey. Section 6 compares 4 Alabama Black Belt counties (Hale, Lowndes, Perry, and Wilcox; Table 1) and conducts an in-depth case study of 1 municipal wastewater system (Uniontown WWTP, Perry County), drawing on 76 ADEM non-compliance citations (2005-2018), sanitary sewer overflow self-reports (Dec 2017-Jan 2019; plus >2,100 statewide ADEM overflows in 2018), engineering reports, personal observations (2016-2018), and unpublished March 2018 water samples.
sample_size.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 11-19, Section 6; Table 1, PDF p. 12

study_design.comment: Published in a philosophy journal without a formal methods section; combines normative political philosophy and constitutional/treaty text review (Sections 1-5) with a single-region/municipality documentary case study of regulatory and municipal sanitation failure in Alabama's Black Belt and Uniontown WWTP using administrative enforcement filings, engineering reports, secondary health studies, and field observations (Section 6).
study_design.value: Normative political philosophy essay and legal-regulatory case study (comparative constitutional review and documentary enforcement case study)
study_design.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 2-3, Section 1; PDF pp. 11-20, Section 6
